stackOverflowQuestions.title: Why does MSVC compile a structured binding of `std::pair<int, float>` worse in `/std:c++20` than in `/std:c++latest`?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: With MSVC x64 /O2 , this function: #include <utility> float bindPair( std::pair<int, float> * s, int i ) { const auto [a, b] = s[i]; return a + b; } compiles differently depending on the language mode ( https://godbolt.org/z/jhv6jf8aa ). /std:c++20 : the pair is loaded into a general-purpose register, stored to a stack temporary, and the float is read back from there: mov rdx, QWORD PTR [rcx+rax*8] mov QWORD PTR $T1[rsp], rdx ... cvtdq2ps xmm0, xmm0 addss xmm0, DWORD PTR $T1[rsp+4] /std:c++latest : both members are read directly from memory, as I would expect: ... cvtdq2ps xmm0, xmm0 addss xmm0, DWORD PTR [rcx+rax*8+4] This matters in a hot loop: when s[i] was just written with two 4-byte stores, the 8-byte reload defeats store-to-load forwarding, and our ray casting got about 15% slower. Which change makes the hidden copy of the pair different in /std:c++latest ?

stackOverflowQuestions.title: How to handle echo vs. genuine speech for barge-in in an Asterisk-based IVR?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I have a doubt regarding how to properly implement a reliable barge-in (speech interruption) mechanism in an Asterisk-based custom voice bot application, where an external Python backend handles conversation flow, TTS, and STT. The core issue we are trying to solve is managing echo and audio quality . When the bot speaks, the caller's phone microphone picks up the audio from the earpiece/speaker, meaning standard talk or sound detection triggers false positives constantly. We are looking at a few different ways people handle this setup, but I am running into some conceptual doubts about how to handle the flow cleanly. Here is what our current design options look like: How we are looking at the options & implementation details: AudioSocket-Only Approach: Python handles both inbound and outbound audio over a single AudioSocket connection. For detection, it checks incoming 20 ms frames against audio levels, speech characteristics, and recent bot audio, running a 5-out-of-10-frame voting decision during an initial learning period to identify interruptions before cancelling TTS and clearing the queue. AudioSocket + AMI Mute Approach: Uses Asterisk's TALK_DETECT ( ChannelTalkingStarted event) as a trigger. Python validates the next caller-audio frame to check for echo, and if it's real speech, issues an AMI command ( MuteAudio ) to mute outbound audio. (The frame-inspection logic acts as a backup if Asterisk doesn't report talking). ARI + AudioSocket Approach: Asterisk handles bot audio playback via ARI (playing WAV chunks), while caller audio streams to Python via a separate, receive-only AudioSocket connection. Python runs a similar frame-check logic (using a 4-out-of-8 frame decision ) and issues a DELETE /playbacks/{id} via ARI to cancel active and queued playbacks upon interruption.
